fields.h1: What Is the Baptism of the Holy Spirit?
fields.meta_title: What Is the Baptism of the Holy Spirit? A Plain Answer
fields.description: Few subjects stir more confusion than the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Here is what Scripture actually says it is, what it is for, and how to receive the Spirit's fullness.
fields.body_html:
Few subjects have caused more confusion, and more longing, than the baptism of the Holy Spirit. Some Christians speak of it as a dramatic second experience; others hardly speak of it at all. Behind the debates, though, is a real hunger — the sense that there must be more to the Christian life than we have known, a power and nearness of God we read about in Scripture but do not always feel. So what did Jesus and the apostles actually mean? Here is a plain attempt to answer, and to point you toward the fullness God genuinely offers.

The promise Jesus made

Before he ascended, Jesus told his followers to wait: “you will be baptized with the Holy Spirit not many days from now” (Acts 1:5). And he told them what it was for: “you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses” (Acts 1:8). Notice the purpose. The baptism of the Spirit is not primarily about a private thrill; it is about power for a mission — to know Christ and to make him known.

The promise was kept at Pentecost. The same fearful disciples who had scattered at Jesus’ arrest were suddenly filled, bold, and unstoppable (Acts 2). Peter, who had denied his Lord to a servant girl weeks earlier, stood before a hostile crowd and preached Christ without a flinch. Something had changed — not their theology but their power. The Spirit they had been promised had come, and men who had been hiding behind locked doors turned the world upside down. That contrast is the whole point. The difference between the disciples before Pentecost and after was not more information or more effort; it was the Spirit’s fullness. And it is exactly that difference — between knowing about God and being filled with him — that so many Christians sense they are missing.

What it is: God himself, within you

At its root, the baptism of the Spirit is the gift of God’s own presence taking up residence in a person. Jesus had pictured it as an inner spring: “Whoever believes in me, as the Scripture has said, ‘Out of his heart will flow rivers of living water.’ Now this he said about the Spirit, whom those who believed in him were to receive” (John 7:38–39). It is not water in a bucket, carried from outside, but a fountain rising from within.

Paul makes clear that in one sense every believer has already received the Spirit: “For in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13), and “anyone who does not have the Spirit of Christ does not belong to him” (Romans 8:9). You cannot be a Christian at all without the Spirit. So the Spirit’s presence is not the private possession of a spiritual elite. If you belong to Christ, he is in you.

Why then do so many feel powerless?

If every believer has the Spirit, why does Scripture keep urging Christians to more? Because there is a difference between having the Spirit and being filled by him — between the Spirit residing in us and the Spirit ruling us. Paul commands, “do not get drunk with wine … but be filled with the Spirit” (Ephesians 5:18). The tense is continuous: go on being filled. This is not a one-time event to collect and file away but a daily yielding, a repeated surrender of more of ourselves to more of God.

R. A. Torrey, who wrote two of the clearest books on this subject — The Baptism with the Holy Spirit and The Person and Work of the Holy Spirit — insisted that this fullness is not for a special class of Christian but is the birthright of every believer, and the great secret of a fruitful life. Torrey had watched ordinary, timid Christians become bold witnesses once they stopped striving in their own strength and received the Spirit’s. Catherine Booth, co-founder of the Salvation Army, preached the same in her sermon The Holy Ghost: that the church’s weakness is almost always, at bottom, an unclaimed promise.

One baptism, or many fillings?

Here is where sincere Christians differ, and it is worth naming plainly. Some traditions teach that the baptism of the Spirit is a distinct second experience after conversion; others teach that it happens at conversion and what follows are repeated fillings. Much of the disagreement is about words more than realities. Scripture uses “baptized,” “filled,” “received,” and “came upon” with some overlap, and godly people have landed in different places.

But under the terminology, the thing itself is not in doubt, and it is what matters. Every believer, at conversion, is united to Christ and indwelt by his Spirit — that is settled (Romans 8:9; 1 Corinthians 12:13). And every believer is then called to go on being filled, surrendering more and more fully to the Spirit’s control (Ephesians 5:18). Whether you call a decisive later surrender a “second blessing” or simply a fuller yielding, the practical counsel is identical: do not settle for less of God than he offers. The disciples were already Christ’s before Pentecost, and yet Pentecost changed them. Do not let a debate about labels talk you out of the experience itself. The danger for most of us is not that we will over-claim the Spirit’s fullness, but that we will quietly make do without it.

What the fullness produces

How do you know the Spirit is at work? Not chiefly by spectacular experiences, real as some are, but by two unmistakable marks. The first is power for witness — a boldness and an effectiveness in pointing others to Christ that is plainly more than natural (Acts 1:8). The second is Christlike character: “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). A person full of the Spirit becomes, over time, more like Jesus. Any “baptism” that produces pride, division, or a loveless spirit has misunderstood the One whose fruit begins with love.

How to receive it

If this fullness is God’s gift and God’s command, how do we lay hold of it? The New Testament pattern is strikingly simple, and it is the pattern Torrey pressed on inquirers:

  • Ask. Jesus said, “how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). This is a prayer God delights to answer.
  • Repent and get clean. The Spirit fills what is surrendered. Sin knowingly held onto is the great hindrance; confession and turning make room.
  • Surrender. Being filled means being ruled. It is the yielding of the whole self — ambitions, fears, plans — to the Spirit’s control.
  • Trust and obey. Do not wait for a feeling before you believe you have received. Take God at his word and step out to obey; the power is proved in the going, not before it.

A word to the disappointed: some who read this have asked, surrendered, and waited — and felt little. Do not conclude God has withheld himself, or that the promise is for others and not for you. His fullness is often quiet, known less by a rush of feeling in a moment than by its fruit over the following weeks: a new steadiness, a love that surprises you, a boldness where there was fear. Feelings are a poor gauge of the Spirit; character and usefulness are the true ones. Keep asking, keep yielding, keep obeying. God is not teasing you. “If you then, who are evil, know how to give good gifts to your children, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him!” (Luke 11:13). The Father is more eager to fill than you are to be filled.

The heart of it

Strip away the controversies and this is the offer at the center: the God who made you wants to fill you with himself, so that you can live a life plainly beyond your own resources — loving people you could not love, facing what you could not face, telling others about a Christ who has become unmistakably real to you. That is not reserved for the few. It is Christ’s promise to all who will ask, surrender, and believe. If you sense there is more, you are right — and the more is not a technique to master but a Person to receive.

The early church was born not out of clever strategy but out of a room full of ordinary people filled with the Spirit of God, and every genuine awakening since has traced back to the same source. The church has never lacked programs, talent, or plans; what it has often lacked is power — the plain, God-given power that turns timid disciples into witnesses and cold hearts warm. That power is not a relic of the first century. It is the standing promise of Christ to his people in every age, yours for the asking. Do not be content to admire it in the book of Acts. Ask for it, yield to it, and go.
